title: What is a stack — a box where you can only add/remove from the TOP (Last In First Out — LIFO), like a stack of plates.

s1_definition.profdef: A stack is a linear data structure that follows Last In First Out ordering, meaning the most recently added element is the first one removed. It supports three core operations: push to add to the top, pop to remove and return the top, and peek to look at the top without removing it. All three are O(1). Stacks are used for undo features, expression evaluation, and tracking method calls.
s1_definition.analogy: A stack is like a pile of transaction receipts on Rajesh's desk at National Bank of India. He always places a new receipt on top of the pile, and when he needs one he takes it from the top. The receipt he picks up is always the last one he put down. He cannot pull a receipt from the middle without removing the ones above it first.
s1_definition.oneliner: A stack is Last In First Out — you only add and remove from the top, like a pile of plates.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** A stack is a linear data structure that follows Last In First Out ordering, meaning the most recently added element is the first one removed. It supports three core operations: push to add to the top, pop to remove and return the top, and peek to look at the top without removing it. All three are O(1). Stacks are used for undo features, expression evaluation, and tracking method calls.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** A stack is like a pile of transaction receipts on Rajesh's desk at National Bank of India. He always places a new receipt on top of the pile, and when he needs one he takes it from the top. The receipt he picks up is always the last one he put down. He cannot pull a receipt from the middle without removing the ones above it first.

**One line to remember:** A stack is Last In First Out — you only add and remove from the top, like a pile of plates.

sections.s2_technical:
The three operations define the stack. Push places a new element on top, becoming the new top. Pop removes and returns the current top, exposing the element beneath it. Peek returns the top without removing it, so you can inspect it. There is no operation to reach into the middle; that restriction is the whole point and is what makes a stack so predictable.

The Last In First Out behaviour is why stacks model so many real problems. The classic example is undo: the last action you did is the first one undone. Another is balanced-bracket checking, where you push each opening bracket and pop when you see a closing one. The Java Virtual Machine itself uses a call stack: when a method is called, a frame is pushed, and when it returns, the frame is popped, which is why infinite recursion causes a StackOverflowError.

In Java you can use the legacy `java.util.Stack` class, but the recommended choice is `java.util.ArrayDeque` used as a stack via its push, pop, and peek methods, because it is faster and not synchronised. You should check `isEmpty` before popping or peeking, because popping an empty stack throws an exception. A senior nuance is that the old Stack class extends Vector and is synchronised, which makes it slower and exposes methods that break the stack abstraction, so modern code prefers ArrayDeque.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — National Bank of India lets Rajesh undo his most recent pending actions, such as adding a payee, in reverse order. The system must store actions so the last one added is the first one undone. This is exactly how a stack works with Last In First Out ordering.

Problem 2 — Trying to undo when there are no actions left must not crash. This is exactly why we check isEmpty before popping and handle the empty case gracefully.

The code has an `ActionStack` class wrapping an ArrayDeque, with push, pop, and peek. The demo pushes a few actions and undoes them, showing the LIFO order.

sections.s5_journey:
Input: three pushes in order ADD_PAYEE Priya, SET_LIMIT 50000, ENABLE_SMS_ALERT.

Step 1 — push ADD_PAYEE Priya: stack top is ADD_PAYEE Priya.

Step 2 — push SET_LIMIT 50000: stack top is SET_LIMIT 50000.

Step 3 — push ENABLE_SMS_ALERT: stack top is ENABLE_SMS_ALERT.

Step 4 — peek returns ENABLE_SMS_ALERT, the most recently pushed, without removing it.

Step 5 — The undo loop pops the top repeatedly: first ENABLE_SMS_ALERT, then SET_LIMIT 50000, then ADD_PAYEE Priya, which is the reverse of the push order, demonstrating Last In First Out.

Step 6 — The stack is now empty, so safePop returns the message nothing to undo instead of throwing.

```
2026-10-26 18:58:41 [INFO] Top action (peek): ENABLE_SMS_ALERT
2026-10-26 18:58:41 [INFO] Undoing: ENABLE_SMS_ALERT
2026-10-26 18:58:41 [INFO] Undoing: SET_LIMIT 50000
2026-10-26 18:58:41 [INFO] Undoing: ADD_PAYEE Priya
2026-10-26 18:58:41 [INFO] Undo on empty stack handled: nothing to undo
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```text
  push sequence:            stack top
  ADD_PAYEE Priya      →    [ADD_PAYEE Priya]
  SET_LIMIT 50000      →    [SET_LIMIT 50000 | ADD_PAYEE Priya]
  ENABLE_SMS_ALERT     →    [ENABLE_SMS_ALERT | SET_LIMIT | ADD_PAYEE]
    │
    ▼ peek → ENABLE_SMS_ALERT (not removed)
    ▼ pop  → ENABLE_SMS_ALERT
    ▼ pop  → SET_LIMIT 50000
    ▼ pop  → ADD_PAYEE Priya      (LIFO: reverse of push order)
    ▼ safePop on empty → "nothing to undo"
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
A stack is a linear data structure that follows Last In First Out ordering, which means the most recently added element is always the first one removed. It supports three core operations, all of which are constant time: push adds an element to the top, pop removes and returns the top, and peek lets me look at the top without removing it. There is deliberately no way to reach into the middle, and that restriction is exactly what makes a stack so predictable and useful.

In my banking project at National Bank of India, I used a stack to implement an undo feature. As Rajesh performs actions like adding a payee or setting a transfer limit, I push each action onto a stack, and when he taps undo I pop the top, which is always the most recent action. Because of the Last In First Out ordering, the actions are undone in the exact reverse of the order he performed them, which is what users expect from undo.

A couple of points I always add. First, I check whether the stack is empty before popping or peeking, because popping an empty stack throws an exception, so I handle the empty case gracefully and return a message like nothing to undo. Second, in modern Java I use ArrayDeque as my stack rather than the legacy Stack class, because the old Stack class extends Vector and is synchronised, which makes it slower and exposes methods that break the clean stack abstraction. I also mention that the Java Virtual Machine itself uses a call stack for method calls, which is why runaway recursion produces a StackOverflowError.
